key_points.text: Speaker introduces himself as Nitesh and welcomes viewers to his YouTube channel.
Creating videos about real‑life AI is difficult because generative AI evolves extremely fast.
Constant emergence of new models, research papers, and tools makes it hard for a teacher to plan a stable curriculum.
Speaker spent months conducting in‑depth research, planning, and designing the generative AI curriculum.
Today’s video is not an announcement but a journey sharing the speaker’s thought process and the full curriculum he created.
Viewers planning to learn generative AI are urged to watch the entire video for important information.
Speaker aims to convince the audience why learning about generative AI is important today.
Definition: Generative AI is a type of AI that creates new content—such as text, images, music, and even code—by learning patterns from data and mimicking human creativity.
Speaker will read the definition aloud and then discuss it further.
AI research has been ongoing for about 60‑70 years, involving generations of brilliant contributors.
Machine learning is identified as the most impactful AI technique compared to earlier approaches like Symbolic AI, fuzzy logic, evolutionary algorithms, NLP, and computer vision.
Machine learning relies on mathematical calculations and statistics applied to large datasets to learn patterns and make predictions on new data.
Machine learning remains relevant today, evidenced by continued job market demand.
Common machine learning problem types include regression (predicting numeric values like stock prices), classification (categorizing items such as cat vs dog), and ranking/recommendation systems.
Machine learning is not suitable for problems that require human creativity.
Earlier AI technologies included Symbolic AI (popular in the 1980s), fuzzy logic systems, evolutionary algorithms, natural language processing, and computer vision.
Generative AI can create new text, code, images, and videos, which is its biggest specialty.
Within two years of generative AI's introduction, the claim that AI cannot replace human creativity became false; generative AI now mimics human creativity.
AI landscape hierarchy: Symbolic AI/Expert Systems/Fuzzy Logic → Machine Learning → Deep Learning (neural networks) → Transformer architecture → Generative AI.
Understanding this hierarchy is essential for studying generative AI.
Generative AI is currently the most powerful development in AI.
Generative AI has created the biggest impact in several areas; the speaker will discuss four key domains.
Customer support was historically a costly function requiring many staff to handle increasing queries and complaints.
Generative AI introduced chatbots as a first‑level support layer, reducing the required human staff from about ten to two‑three agents.
Modern companies now deploy a chatbot as the first contact point, followed by a smaller human support team, improving efficiency and lowering costs.
Content creation was previously thought to be beyond AI’s reach, but generative AI now assists in creating content.
Generative AI is expected to heavily penetrate the content creation industry and can be applied in any form.
Generative AI tools can produce content such as articles that are indistinguishable from human writing.
Content creation is a domain where AI penetration is already high and will continue to grow.
Education is being transformed as AI can act as a personal tutor, answering questions and providing practice problems.
Schools need to evolve and implement educational methods that incorporate AI tools.
Generative AI can write production‑ready code, reducing the need for many programmers and accelerating software development.
When stuck on curriculum planning or coding problems, the speaker can consult ChatGPT as a personal tutor.
The speaker is uncertain whether a Medium article was written by a human or by AI, highlighting the quality of AI‑generated content.
Two or three programmers can handle a task easily, indicating a manageable workload.
Generative AI is identified as a major impact area.
Before investing time in a technology, it must be evaluated for real‑world problem solving.
The speaker will compare generative AI’s success with that of the internet and blockchain/crypto.
The internet is considered a highly successful technology because it solves real‑world problems such as communication, banking, travel, and shopping.
Blockchain and crypto are technologies of the speaker’s lifetime that have not yet reached their full potential.
A technology is deemed successful if it answers "yes" to the first evaluation question: Is it real‑world and does it solve a problem?
The speaker will present a series of evaluation questions to the audience to determine technology success.
The internet enables solving problems remotely from a phone at home.
Speaker notes a lack of clear real‑world problems solved by cryptocurrency.
Generative AI solves the customer‑support problem faced by companies worldwide.
Generative AI provides personal tutoring, addressing education challenges.
Generative AI is useful on a daily basis and can be employed regularly.
China’s new AI model DeepSeek R1 caused a massive impact on stock markets.
AI creates new technical jobs despite concerns about job displacement.
AI engineers have emerged as a new job category.
Demand for AI-related roles is growing daily and could become as popular as software development within five years.
Generative AI tools are easily accessible and can be used by non‑technical users, including parents, without writing code.
Time is ticking; there is a good chance AI job roles will become as popular as software development in the next five years.
Generative AI has not yet reached its full potential; investing time and effort now is advisable for future benefits.
When generative AI reaches its full potential, those working in AI will benefit significantly.
The speaker delayed posting videos about generative AI because of initial doubts about the technology, its novelty, and limited experience.
Generative AI is emphasized as important for the future, and the speaker encourages audience engagement with the content.
Generative AI could be a powerful technology or just a hype bubble.
Initial barrier to learning generative AI was limited time and other life responsibilities.
After finding time, the speaker now teaches generative AI and creates mass video content.
Rapid daily emergence of new models, tools, papers, and terminology creates fear and overwhelm.
Information overload makes it difficult to find meaningful content and learn AI correctly.
Doubts about generative AI have been resolved after sufficient learning; confidence to commit time again.
Tracking daily advancements and extracting meaning remains a challenging task.
Constant discussion of new AI developments creates a FOMO environment.
Teaching Generative AI effectively starts with designing a solid curriculum.
Without a central concept, creating a good curriculum for Generative AI is difficult.
A mental model is introduced to simplify information overload in Generative AI.
Foundation Models are identified as the central term for the Generative AI mental model.
Foundation Models are large‑scale AI models trained on massive internet‑wide data.
Training Foundation Models requires huge financial investment, extensive data, and many GPUs.
Unlike specialized ML models, Foundation Models are generalized and can be applied broadly.
The speaker leverages prior experience in machine learning and deep learning to build mental models.
Task-specific models are designed for a single task (e.g., stock price prediction) and cannot generalize to other tasks like cricket score prediction.
Foundation models are generalized AI models with large architectures and many parameters, trained on massive data, enabling them to solve multiple tasks across domains.
Large Language Models (LLMs) are a type of foundation model that can perform diverse tasks such as text generation, sentiment analysis, summarization, and question answering.
During training, LLMs learn multiple capabilities by predicting the next word on internet-scale data, which also imparts skills like sentiment analysis and question answering.
Foundation models are not limited to text; large multimodal models also exist that can process and generate content for text, images, videos, and audio.
Today's generative AI landscape is built on foundation models, which serve as the backbone for many applications.
Generative AI can be divided into two parts: using foundation models and building foundation models.
The foundation model is the core component at the center of the entire generative AI system.
Two perspectives exist: the user perspective (using foundation models) and the builder perspective (creating foundation models).
The mental model simplifies the understanding of generative AI by focusing on foundation models.
The speaker claims to be the first to introduce this mental model and associated terminology.
To apply the model, ask ChatGPT to define a new term (e.g., "promoted engineering") and then decide whether it belongs to the user side or the builder side.
Prompt engineering enables users to ask an LLM in English and refine prompts to obtain better answers.
Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) is a technology that can complete an LLM, modify its behavior, and safeguard it from generating inappropriate content.
Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) allows an LLM to answer questions using private documents or data.
Pre-training involves training a foundation model on large, global datasets using substantial hardware resources.
Quantization is the process of creating an optimized model that can run efficiently in different environments.
AI Agents are software systems built with LLMs that can answer questions and perform tasks such as booking tickets.
Vector databases are useful for implementing RAG and managing embeddings for private data retrieval.

Builder perspective vs. User perspective: LLM development steps (prompt engineering, RLHF, RAG, pre-training, quantization) are handled by builders, while end users interact with the final LLM or AI agents.
Fine‑tuning applies to both the building and the using side of LLMs.
The speaker created a curriculum that covers two perspectives: builders and users.
Builder side curriculum must include fundamentals of machine learning and deep learning.
Knowledge of a deep learning framework is required; PyTorch is preferred over TensorFlow.
The curriculum starts with transformer architecture because all modern foundation models are built on it.
Builders must understand encoder side, decoder side, embeddings, self‑attention layer, and normalization in language modeling.
The builder side is technical and most relevant for those already working in machine learning.
Fundamentals should be covered early before moving to advanced topics.
Multiple types of transformers exist, including encoder‑only, decoder‑only, and encoder‑decoder architectures.
A solid understanding of transformer architecture is required, including GPT and other famous transformer models.
Pre‑training is the first phase for foundation models, where you define training objectives and tokenization strategy.
Training can be performed on cloud resources or distributed across multiple machines; appropriate infrastructure choices are essential.
Large‑scale model training presents many challenges; knowing these challenges and their solutions is critical.
After pre‑training, evaluation is performed to assess how well the model meets its objectives.
Optimization reduces the size of large foundation models for deployment on standard hardware, using techniques such as compression and model pruning.
Knowledge distillation is included in the curriculum after quantization.
Making predictions consumes LLM time; optimization is used to reduce this overhead.
The curriculum consists of modules: optimization, fine‑tuning, evaluation, and deployment.
Foundation models are trained on large datasets, resulting in generalized capabilities.
Fine‑tuning adapts a generalized model to a specific task to improve performance.
Instruction tuning is a form of continuous pre‑training for domain‑specific adaptation.
RLAF is a technique used in domain‑specific pre‑training.
PFT (Parameter Fine Tuning) is referenced as a relevant technique.
Evaluation must be thorough before deployment; metrics are used to assess model performance.
Deep Seek LLM outperforms other models (R1, Cha, GPD) according to community votes.
Decision‑making involves analyzing different metrics and model performance.
Deployment is the final and critical step in the model lifecycle.
To build a foundation model, start by using a ready-made foundation model.
The curriculum includes a user side where learners focus on using foundation models rather than building them.
Building foundation models is more difficult than using them; the user side is easier and more fun.
First learning objective in LLM: create basic applications using foundation models.
Foundation models can be closed source or open source; closed source models are accessed via APIs.
For closed source models, use tools like Hugging Face library to operate the LLM on your machine or run it locally with tools such as Ouma.
Learn frameworks like LangChain to build LLM-based applications; Hugging Face Llama is an example.
After basic usage, the important stage is improving LLM responses; three techniques are involved, starting with prompt engineering.
If you fail, refer to the builder's perspective; all steps are listed.
Promotion engineering is the first method to improve the output of an LLM.
RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) lets an LLM access personal data and answer questions using private information.
Fine-tuning can be done on the builder side or user side, at varying depths (shallow to deep layers), allowing customization of model behavior.
AI agents are an emerging field where LLMs power bots that perform tasks like booking hotels and giving travel recommendations, beyond simple chat.
Promotion, RAG, and fine-tuning are the three primary techniques discussed for enhancing LLM output.
To build LLM applications, you need tools and a chatbot plus tools to create AI agents.
LLM Ops is an umbrella term covering evaluation, improvements, and technical handling of deployed LLM applications.
Libraries are available to assist with LLM Ops tasks.
Multimodal inputs such as audio and video can be incorporated into LLM applications.
Diffusion-based models like Stable Diffusion are part of the broader AI ecosystem.
The curriculum for learning LLM application development is divided into builder side and user side.
The field of LLM applications and LLM Ops is rapidly growing.
Understanding both builder and user perspectives is essential for developing effective LLM applications.
AI development has two sides: the builder side (creating foundation models/LLMs) and the user side (building applications).
Knowing both builder and user side skills allows professionals to demand higher salaries and become versatile AI engineers.
The curriculum is divided into builder and user sides and will be covered in parallel to minimize overlap.
To become a research scientist focus on the builder side; to become an AI engineer focus on both builder and user sides simultaneously.
Anyone can create LLM‑based applications with even a little knowledge; software development shares about 80‑85% of the process.
Understanding how foundation models are built improves performance on the user side and can lead to becoming a software developer.
Speaker has studied architecture and has covered deep learning playlist including encoder‑only, decoder‑only transformers, and will teach decoder‑based transformers such as GPT.
Plan to create a dedicated playlist with small, manageable modules instead of a single large playlist.
Will cover both builder and user sides of LLM applications, including pre‑training, fine‑tuning, RAG, and will release a basic LLM applications playlist by the end of the month.
Explanation for not running paid courses: receives many requests, big ad tech companies approached for generative AI courses, but prefers free content and small‑chunk delivery.
Emphasis on small commitment and breaking material into tiny chunks to avoid overwhelming learners.
The speaker is currently using the technology 100% and plans to create a paid course only after mastering it completely.
Goal: to understand the technology inside out, teach others, and become an expert.
YouTube is used to reach a wide audience, gather feedback, and improve content based on viewer responses.
The speaker has already published several YouTube videos and will release a major announcement and additional videos soon.
Planned video production schedule: 2‑3 videos per week, with one large video covering multiple topics each week.
Rough timeline estimate: mastering the entire subject will take about one full year.
Speaker promises to remove free content after the paid course is released, indicating a future shift to paid-only material.
Personal motivation: the speaker is excited, curious, and aims to become an expert, seeing learning as a powerful experience.
Speaker invites feedback and suggestions from the audience to improve the content.
The presenter invites viewers to leave comments in the comment section.
The series begins with the goal to learn and master Generative AI.
Viewers are asked to like, share, and subscribe if they enjoy the video.
The presenter signs off and mentions the next video.
